messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
Let M be a metric space with distance d, and let (F_n) be a decreasing sequence of nonempty closed sets with diam F_n tending to 0.
Does completeness force this nested family to have a nonempty intersection?
It does, because choosing x_n in F_n for every n makes d(x_m, x_n) <= diam F_n for all m > n, and diam F_n tends to 0, so (x_n) is Cauchy.
Completeness gives a limit x in M.
For each n, the terms x_k with k >= n lie in the closed set F_n and converge to x, so x belongs to every F_n, and the intersection is nonempty.
Must this property characterize completeness rather than merely imply it?
It does, because for any Cauchy sequence (y_n) the closed sets G_n = closure of {y_k : k >= n} are nonempty, decreasing, and have diameters tending to 0, since closure does not change diameter and the tail diameters of a Cauchy sequence tend to 0; for any positive radius r, choosing a sufficiently large N ensures that the common point x, which lies in every G_n, is within r/2 of some tail element y_m, and the Cauchy property then keeps all terms from N onward within r of x, so x is a limit of (y_n).
Is that enough to show every Cauchy sequence converges?
Yes, every Cauchy sequence converges to such a point x, so M is complete, and the equivalence is proved.
